newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Italy seen joining ERM, trailing on EMU.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Italy seen joining ERM, trailing on EMU.

text.p: Italy is widely expected to rejoin Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) by the end of this year but its ambition to be a founder member of the single currency club is likely to be thwarted, Reuters surveys show.

In the first quarterly Reuters poll of how Europe is shaping up for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), 25 out of 27 specialists said they believed the Italian lira, which fell out of the ERM in September 1992, would rejoin by end December.

But in a monthly survey asking which of the 15 European countries would be in the first round of EMU, due to start on January 1, 1999, 38 out of 41 contributors said they expected Italy to be excluded.

"Within the mainstream of European currencies, the lira is regarded as the weakest. It will be impossible to convince the (German) population to give up the mark and accept a new currency which includes the lira," said Klaus Baader, senior European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
For Italy to be eligible under the rules for currency union, the lira has to move within 15 percent of its central rate against the German mark for two years prior to January 1999.
Of the other EU nations currently outside the ERM, none of the experts expected Britain or Greece to join and only two out of 19 expected Sweden to be within the ERM by end-1996.
In the early 1990s, a loss of confidence caused by political and economic woes caused widespread unloading of Italian assets.

The lira was forced to withdraw from the ERM after attempts to keep it within the then 2.25 percent range of the central rate against the mark ran into problems. ERM rules have since changed and member currencies are now allowed to move 15 percent either side of the central rate against the mark.
The lira has assumed stability since this year's general election and the appointment of Romano Prodi as prime minister of a left-leaning coalition.
According to the Reuters quarterly survey, Italy will meet the EMU entry criteria on low inflation and low long-term interest rates.

Eighteen out of 21 participants said they expected Italy's long-term interest rates to fall within an acceptable range -- less than two percent above the rates prevailing in the three member states with lowest levels of inflation.
Seventeen out of 23 experts expected Italy's 1997 inflation to be within 1.5 percent of the average prevailing in the three member states with the lowest inflation rates.
But Italy will fail to keep its budget deficit or public debt within the target limits, according to the survey.

Thirteen out of 25 expect the Italian budget deficit to be between 3.5 and 4.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- the target is three percent -- and 23 out of 25 expect total debt to be over the criterion of 60 percent of GDP.
Earlier in November the European Commission forecast Italy's budget deficit at 3.3 percent of GDP for 1997 and total indebtedness to GDP at 122.3 percent.
But although Italy may be close to some of the EMU criteria, Germany will do all it can to keep Italy out, analysts say.
David Naude, economist for France at JP Morgan said: "The track record for Italy with a stable budget, a stable economy and stable inflation will be too short".
Some analysts fear that if Italy is left out at the start, it will vote against EMU and the whole project will be derailed.
The vote is due to be taken early 1998.

For EMU to go ahead a majority of 62 votes out of a total of 87 split among EU member states are needed. Italy has 10 votes which, if added to other possible "no' votes, could in theory swing the balance.
But Deutsche's Baader believes voting against may be counter-productive to Italian interests.
"They will want to join at a later stage and there are benefits of stable long-term interest rates derived from market expectations that Italy will eventually join," he said.
